constitutional_provisions.text: The United Kingdom does not have a single codified constitutional document. There is no explicit constitutional provision mentioning future generations or intergenerational equity at the UK level. However, the UK is bound by international obligations including the European Convention on Human Rights (via the Human Rights Act 1998) and the Paris Agreement, which have been interpreted by courts as carrying intergenerational dimensions.

dedicated_legislation.name: Well-being of Future Generations (Wales) Act 2015
dedicated_legislation.summary: Landmark Welsh legislation requiring public bodies to carry out sustainable development in pursuit of seven well-being goals (prosperous, resilient, healthier, more equal, cohesive communities, vibrant culture, globally responsible Wales). Public bodies must take account of the long term, prevent problems, take integrated and collaborative approaches, and involve people of all ages. Wales is the only country in the world with a legally binding Well-being of Future Generations Act.

dedicated_legislation.name: Wellbeing of Future Generations Bill [HL] 2021-22
dedicated_legislation.status: proposed (did not progress past second reading)
dedicated_legislation.summary: Private member's bill introduced by Lord Bird (Crossbench) inspired by the Wales Act. Proposed national wellbeing goals, a Commission for Future Generations for the UK, future generations impact assessments for public bodies, preventative spending accounting, and extending the Office for Budget Responsibility's duties to include intergenerational reporting. Did not progress beyond second reading in the House of Lords.

dedicated_legislation.name: Wellbeing of Future Generations (No. 2) Bill 2022
dedicated_legislation.summary: Second attempt at a UK-wide future generations bill, also introduced by Lord Bird. Similar provisions to the 2021 bill. Did not progress.

dedicated_legislation.name: Climate Change Act 2008
dedicated_legislation.summary: Legally binding carbon budgets and a 2050 net zero target (amended 2019). While not explicitly framed as intergenerational equity legislation, the carbon budgeting mechanism inherently protects future generations by requiring long-term emissions reduction pathways. The Act created the independent Climate Change Committee to advise on carbon budgets.

institutional_mechanisms.name: Future Generations Commissioner for Wales
institutional_mechanisms.mandate: Independent statutory role established under the Well-being of Future Generations (Wales) Act 2015. Acts as a guardian for the interests of future generations in Wales, monitoring and reporting on how public bodies implement the Act's sustainable development principle. Can conduct reviews, make recommendations, and provide advice to public bodies. Current Commissioner: Derek Walker.

institutional_mechanisms.name: House of Lords Select Committee on Intergenerational Fairness and Provision
institutional_mechanisms.mandate: Special inquiry committee established to consider intergenerational fairness and provision across the UK. Published a comprehensive report in April 2019 recommending Intergenerational Impact Assessments for all draft legislation, generational distributional analysis of budgets, and improved data collection on intergenerational fairness. The committee dissolved after publishing its report.

institutional_mechanisms.name: Climate Change Committee (CCC)
institutional_mechanisms.mandate: Independent statutory body established under the Climate Change Act 2008. Advises the UK government on emissions targets, carbon budgets, and adaptation. Its long-term carbon budget framework inherently serves intergenerational equity by ensuring emissions reduction pathways extend decades into the future. Reports to Parliament annually on progress.

institutional_mechanisms.name: Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR)
institutional_mechanisms.mandate: Independent fiscal watchdog that produces long-term fiscal sustainability reports analysing public finances over a 50-year horizon. The Wellbeing of Future Generations Bill proposed extending OBR's duties to include explicit intergenerational reporting, but this has not been enacted.

judicial_precedents.case: R (Friends of the Earth) v Secretary of State for International Trade / UK Export Finance [2022] EWHC 568 (Admin)
judicial_precedents.court: High Court of England and Wales (Administrative Court)
judicial_precedents.relevance: Challenge to UK Export Finance's decision to finance a LNG project in Mozambique. The court was split: one judge found the government had no rational basis to conclude the financing was consistent with Paris Agreement Article 2(1)(c), while the other judge disagreed. The Court of Appeal [2023] EWCA Civ 14 dismissed the appeal, ruling that UK domestic courts cannot determine whether the UK has violated unincorporated international treaty obligations. This case illustrates the limits of UK courts in enforcing intergenerational climate obligations through international law.
judicial_precedents.outcome: Claim dismissed on appeal. Split decision at High Court.

judicial_precedents.case: R (Plan B Earth) v Secretary of State for Transport [2020] EWCA Civ 214 (Heathrow third runway)
judicial_precedents.court: Court of Appeal of England and Wales
judicial_precedents.relevance: The Court of Appeal ruled that the government's Airports National Policy Statement was unlawful because it failed to consider the Paris Agreement commitments. While later overturned by the Supreme Court, the Court of Appeal's reasoning acknowledged the relevance of long-term climate obligations. Relevant to intergenerational equity as it concerned infrastructure decisions with multi-decade impacts.
judicial_precedents.outcome: Initially successful at Court of Appeal; overturned by Supreme Court in December 2020.

international_commitments.instrument: UN Declaration on Future Generations (Pact for the Future, Annex II)
international_commitments.relevant_clause: The UK, as a UN member state, adopted the Declaration on Future Generations at the Summit of the Future on 22 September 2024. The Declaration commits states to take long-term perspectives in decision-making, safeguard the needs and interests of future generations, and strengthen intergenerational equity in policy frameworks.

international_commitments.instrument: Paris Agreement (UNFCCC)
international_commitments.relevant_clause: Article 2(1)(c) commits parties to 'making finance flows consistent with a pathway towards low greenhouse gas emissions and climate-resilient development.' The Agreement's preamble acknowledges 'intergenerational equity' as a guiding principle. The UK ratified the Paris Agreement on 17 November 2016.

international_commitments.instrument: European Convention on Human Rights (via Human Rights Act 1998)
international_commitments.relevant_clause: Article 2 (right to life) and Article 8 (right to private and family life) have been interpreted by the European Court of Human Rights as carrying positive obligations on states to protect against environmental harm, including for future generations. The UK incorporated the ECHR via the Human Rights Act 1998.

policy_integration.mechanism: Intergenerational Impact Assessments (proposed, not enacted)
policy_integration.description: The House of Lords Intergenerational Fairness and Provision Committee recommended that the UK Government create Intergenerational Impact Assessments for all draft legislation, indicating how it will affect different generations. The government has not implemented this recommendation. The Wellbeing of Future Generations Bill also proposed mandatory future generations impact assessments, but the bill did not pass.

policy_integration.mechanism: OBR Fiscal Sustainability Report (50-year horizon)
policy_integration.description: The Office for Budget Responsibility produces an annual Fiscal Sustainability Report projecting public finances over a 50-year horizon, including demographic pressures, health spending, and pension obligations. This provides a long-term lens on fiscal policy, though it is not explicitly framed as intergenerational equity analysis.

policy_integration.mechanism: Wales Well-being Goals and Sustainable Development Principle
policy_integration.description: Under the Well-being of Future Generations (Wales) Act, all public bodies in Wales must set and publish well-being objectives aligned with the seven national well-being goals, apply the five ways of working (long-term, prevention, integration, collaboration, involvement), and report annually. The Future Generations Commissioner monitors compliance. This is the most comprehensive policy integration mechanism for intergenerational equity in the UK.

countries.notes: The UK presents a mixed picture. Wales is a global leader with its Well-being of Future Generations Act and Commissioner — the only country with such a comprehensive legal framework. However, at the UK-wide level, there is no codified constitution, no dedicated future generations legislation (two bills failed to progress), and no national commissioner. The UK's strength lies in its climate governance infrastructure (Climate Change Act, CCC, carbon budgets) and fiscal long-term analysis (OBR), which indirectly serve intergenerational equity. The House of Lords committee's 2019 recommendations for Intergenerational Impact Assessments remain unimplemented. UK courts have been reluctant to enforce international climate obligations domestically (FoE v UKEF), limiting judicial enforcement of intergenerational climate duties.

constitutional_provisions.text: The Constitution expressly embeds environmental stewardship in both the Directive Principles and Fundamental Duties. Article 48A requires the State to protect and improve the environment and safeguard forests and wildlife. Article 51A(g) places a duty on every citizen to protect and improve the natural environment. Together these provisions create a constitutional basis for long-term ecological stewardship even though the Constitution does not explicitly mention future generations.

constitutional_provisions.article: Article 21 as interpreted by the Supreme Court
constitutional_provisions.text: Indian environmental constitutionalism rests heavily on Article 21. Through judicial interpretation, the right to life has been expanded to include the right to a clean, healthy, and safe environment. In 2024 the Supreme Court further held that a right against the adverse effects of climate change flows from Articles 14 and 21, strengthening the constitutional basis for protecting present and future generations from climate harm.

dedicated_legislation.name: Environment (Protection) Act, 1986
dedicated_legislation.summary: Framework environmental legislation enacted after the Bhopal disaster. It gives the Union government broad powers to set environmental standards, regulate hazardous activities, and issue notifications such as the environmental impact assessment regime. While not framed in future-generations language, it is the core statute through which India operationalizes long-term environmental protection.

dedicated_legislation.name: Biological Diversity Act, 2002
dedicated_legislation.summary: Implements the Convention on Biological Diversity in domestic law. It creates a legal structure for conservation, sustainable use, and equitable benefit sharing over biological resources and associated knowledge, making it a key statute for preserving ecological assets over time.

dedicated_legislation.name: National Green Tribunal Act, 2010
dedicated_legislation.summary: Creates a specialized environmental court with powers to hear civil cases relating to environmental protection, forests, biodiversity, and compensation for environmental damage. The Act institutionalizes faster adjudication and the enforcement of sustainability-oriented environmental principles.

institutional_mechanisms.name: National Green Tribunal
institutional_mechanisms.mandate: The National Green Tribunal provides a dedicated forum for environmental adjudication and applies principles such as sustainable development, the precautionary principle, and polluter pays. It is one of the clearest institutional mechanisms India has for translating long-term environmental duties into enforceable remedies.

institutional_mechanisms.name: National Biodiversity Authority
institutional_mechanisms.mandate: Created under the Biological Diversity Act, the National Biodiversity Authority regulates access to biological resources, oversees benefit sharing, and supports conservation governance. Its role is directly tied to preserving biodiversity as a long-term public good rather than a purely extractive present-day asset.

judicial_precedents.case: M.K. Ranjitsinh and Others v Union of India (2024 INSC 280)
judicial_precedents.relevance: The Supreme Court held that a right against the adverse effects of climate change is embedded in Articles 14 and 21. The judgment ties biodiversity protection, energy transition, and constitutional rights together and marks a major step in giving climate harms constitutional status in India.
judicial_precedents.outcome: Climate-related constitutional protection recognized under Articles 14 and 21.

judicial_precedents.case: Vellore Citizens' Welfare Forum v Union of India (1996) 5 SCC 647
judicial_precedents.relevance: This foundational environmental case brought the precautionary principle and polluter pays principle into Indian law and treated sustainable development as part of domestic environmental jurisprudence. It remains one of the strongest doctrinal anchors for balancing development with long-term ecological protection.
judicial_precedents.outcome: Sustainable development, precautionary principle, and polluter pays recognized in Indian environmental law.

judicial_precedents.case: A.P. Pollution Control Board v Prof. M.V. Nayudu (1999) 2 SCC 718
judicial_precedents.relevance: The Court emphasized precaution, scientific uncertainty, and the need for specialized environmental decision-making. The judgment is important because it framed environmental governance as requiring anticipatory protection rather than waiting for irreversible harm.
judicial_precedents.outcome: Precautionary environmental reasoning and the need for expert environmental adjudication reinforced.

international_commitments.instrument: United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change and Paris Agreement
international_commitments.relevant_clause: India is a party to the UNFCCC and Paris Agreement. These frameworks explicitly connect climate protection with equity and the interests of present and future generations. India's nationally determined contribution and climate planning documents are submitted within this framework.

international_commitments.instrument: India's Long-Term Low-Emission Development Strategy (LT-LEDS)
international_commitments.relevant_clause: India's LT-LEDS operationalizes its Paris commitments through a long-horizon development strategy linked to net-zero by 2070, low-carbon growth, adaptation, and climate-resilient development. It is not a treaty in itself, but it is a formal long-term international climate commitment submitted under the UNFCCC process.

international_commitments.instrument: UN Declaration on Future Generations (Pact for the Future, Annex II)
international_commitments.relevant_clause: India adopted the Declaration on Future Generations at the Summit of the Future. The declaration commits states to integrate long-term thinking, evidence, and institutional foresight into governance and to safeguard the needs and interests of generations to come.

policy_integration.mechanism: Environmental Impact Assessment regime under the Environment (Protection) Act
policy_integration.description: India's environmental clearance system, built under the Environment (Protection) Act and subsequent EIA notifications, is the main tool for integrating long-term environmental consequences into project approval. In practice its quality is uneven, but institutionally it is the clearest mechanism for forcing ex ante assessment of environmental harm.

policy_integration.mechanism: National Action Plan on Climate Change and state-level climate planning
policy_integration.description: The National Action Plan on Climate Change and associated state action plans embed longer-term climate and resource considerations into sectoral governance through missions on solar energy, energy efficiency, sustainable habitat, water, Himalayan ecosystems, sustainable agriculture, and knowledge. This is one of India's main policy bridges between environmental protection and development planning.

policy_integration.mechanism: NDC 2031-35 and LT-LEDS long-range climate planning
policy_integration.description: India's current NDC and LT-LEDS embed long-term planning in climate governance through emissions-intensity targets, non-fossil electricity capacity goals, adaptation priorities, and a 2070 net-zero pathway. These instruments do not create a standalone future-generations test, but they do institutionalize multi-decade planning in ways directly relevant to intergenerational equity.

countries.notes: India has one of the stronger constitutional-environmental doctrines in the Global South, even without a standalone future generations act. Its framework rests on a mix of constitutional duties, expansive Article 21 jurisprudence, core environmental statutes, and a specialized environmental tribunal. The strongest recent development is the Supreme Court's 2024 recognition that protection against the adverse effects of climate change flows from Articles 14 and 21. That said, India still lacks a dedicated future generations commissioner or ombudsperson, and the implementation gap is substantial: environmental clearances remain contested, ecological protection is often traded against development imperatives, and intergenerational fairness is not yet systematically embedded in fiscal, youth-participation, or whole-of-government decision processes. In other words, India is doctrinally ambitious but institutionally uneven.

constitutional_provisions.text: The Republic promotes the development of culture and scientific and technical research. It protects the landscape and the historical and artistic heritage of the Nation. The Republic protects the environment, biodiversity and ecosystems, also in the interest of future generations. The law of the State regulates the ways and forms of animal protection.

Private economic initiative is free. It cannot be carried out in contrast with social utility or in such a way as to damage health, the environment, security, freedom and human dignity. The law determines the programmes and controls appropriate so that public and private economic activity can be directed and coordinated to social and environmental purposes.

dedicated_legislation.name: Constitutional Law No. 1/2022 — Amendment of Articles 9 and 41
dedicated_legislation.summary: Landmark constitutional reform passed by the Italian Parliament on 8 February 2022. For the first time in Italy's history, it explicitly introduces the protection of the environment, biodiversity and ecosystems 'in the interest of future generations' as a fundamental principle of the Republic (Article 9). It also amends Article 41 to add health and the environment as constitutional limits on private economic initiative. Italy was one of the first countries in the world to insert 'future generations' explicitly into the fundamental principles of its constitution.

dedicated_legislation.name: National Recovery and Resilience Plan — NRRP (Piano Nazionale di Ripresa e Resilienza, PNRR)
dedicated_legislation.summary: Italy's €191.5 billion recovery plan under the EU NextGenerationEU framework. Explicitly incorporates generational equity as a cross-cutting priority: 'reducing territorial, generational and gender gaps.' Named 'Next Generation Italia' to signal its intergenerational purpose. Commits 37% of spending to green transition investments.

institutional_mechanisms.name: EU Commissioner for Intergenerational Fairness, Youth, Culture and Sport
institutional_mechanisms.mandate: As an EU member state, Italy benefits from the European Commission's newly created portfolio for Intergenerational Fairness, held by Commissioner Glenn Micallef (from 2024). This represents the first explicit EU-level institutional mandate for intergenerational fairness. Italy participated in and supported the creation of this role.

institutional_mechanisms.name: No dedicated national future generations commissioner
institutional_mechanisms.mandate: Italy has no national-level commissioner, ombudsperson, or dedicated parliamentary body specifically for future generations. The 2022 constitutional amendment creates a mandate but no institution to enforce it. Civil society organisations (e.g. A Sud, Greenpeace Italy) are pushing for stronger implementation.

judicial_precedents.case: A Sud et al. v. Italy (Giudizio Universale) — Tribunal of Rome, 26 February 2024
judicial_precedents.court: Civil Court of Rome (Tribunale di Roma)
judicial_precedents.relevance: Italy's first climate litigation case. Filed by 24 NGOs and over 200 private citizens against the Italian state, demanding stronger greenhouse gas emission reductions. Plaintiffs explicitly invoked the rights of future generations under the newly amended Article 9 of the Italian Constitution, as well as the ECHR and EU Charter. The Court dismissed the case on 26 February 2024, finding lack of absolute jurisdiction — ruling that ordering the state to adopt stronger climate policies was a matter for the legislature, not the judiciary. A significant precedent establishing that Article 9's 'future generations' language is now used in litigation, even if this initial case was dismissed on procedural grounds.
judicial_precedents.outcome: Dismissed for lack of jurisdiction (inadmissible). Appeal proceedings and further litigation expected.

judicial_precedents.case: Greenpeace Italy et al. v. ENI et al. — ongoing as of 2025
judicial_precedents.court: Civil Court (jurisdiction confirmed by Italian Supreme Court 2025)
judicial_precedents.relevance: Climate case against ENI (Italy's state oil company), brought by Greenpeace Italy and others. Plaintiffs allege ENI violated their fundamental rights including the rights of future generations protected under the amended Article 9. The Italian Supreme Court confirmed jurisdiction in 2025, allowing the case to proceed. Explicitly invokes Article 9's future generations language against a corporate defendant.
judicial_precedents.outcome: Jurisdiction confirmed by Supreme Court (2025). Case proceeding.

international_commitments.instrument: UN Declaration on Future Generations (Pact for the Future, Annex II)
international_commitments.relevant_clause: Italy, as a UN member state, adopted the Declaration on Future Generations at the Summit of the Future on 22 September 2024.

international_commitments.instrument: Paris Agreement (UNFCCC)
international_commitments.relevant_clause: Italy ratified the Paris Agreement on 11 November 2016. As an EU member state, Italy is bound by EU climate law including the European Climate Law (net-zero by 2050, 55% reduction by 2030). The Paris Agreement preamble acknowledges intergenerational equity.

international_commitments.instrument: EU Climate Law (Regulation 2021/1119)
international_commitments.relevant_clause: As an EU member state, Italy is bound by the European Climate Law which enshrines net-zero by 2050 and a 55% GHG reduction by 2030 into EU law. The preamble references intergenerational equity and the duty to protect future generations.

policy_integration.mechanism: NRRP Generational Equity Cross-Priority
policy_integration.description: Italy's National Recovery and Resilience Plan (PNRR) integrates generational equity as one of three cross-cutting priorities alongside gender equality and territorial rebalancing. All investments are assessed against their contribution to reducing generational gaps. The plan allocates significant resources to youth employment, education, and green transition.

policy_integration.mechanism: Constitutional mandate for future-generations-aware legislation (Art. 9, 2022)
policy_integration.description: The 2022 constitutional amendment creates a mandate for all Italian legislation and public decisions to be interpreted in light of future generations' interests. Legal scholars note this creates a constitutional benchmark against which laws can be challenged, though a specific implementing framework has not yet been enacted.

countries.notes: Italy's headline story is its landmark 2022 constitutional amendment — one of the first countries globally to insert 'future generations' explicitly into the fundamental principles of its constitution (Article 9). This gives the concept constitutional standing at the highest level of the legal order. The judicial picture is nascent but active: the Giudizio Universale case (2024) was dismissed on procedural grounds but used Article 9's future generations language, and the ENI case is proceeding after Supreme Court confirmed jurisdiction in 2025. The main gaps are the absence of a dedicated national institution (no commissioner or ombudsperson) and no specific implementing legislation for the Article 9 mandate beyond the NRRP. Italy also benefits from EU-level architecture — the EU's new Intergenerational Fairness Commissioner and EU Climate Law both strengthen Italy's framework from above.

constitutional_provisions.text: The Australian Constitution (1901) contains no explicit provision on future generations, intergenerational equity, or environmental rights. The Constitution is largely a structural document dividing powers between the Commonwealth and states. Courts have noted it operates as an 'intergenerational compact intended to endure for centuries' (McHugh J in Theophanous v Herald & Weekly Times Ltd), but this has not been used to derive enforceable intergenerational rights.

dedicated_legislation.name: Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act 1999 (EPBC Act) — Intergenerational Equity Principle
dedicated_legislation.summary: Australia's primary national environmental law. Section 3A explicitly enshrines intergenerational equity as one of the core principles of ecologically sustainable development: 'the present generation should ensure that the health, diversity and productivity of the environment is maintained or enhanced for the benefit of future generations.' This is one of the strongest statutory intergenerational equity provisions in Australian law, though it applies primarily to environmental decision-making.

dedicated_legislation.name: Climate Change Act 2022
dedicated_legislation.summary: Australia's first standalone climate change legislation, passed under the Albanese government. Enshrines a 43% emissions reduction target by 2030 and net-zero by 2050 into law. Requires the Climate Change Authority to provide annual progress reports. While not framed as a future generations law, its long-term statutory targets inherently protect future generations by locking in a decarbonisation trajectory.

dedicated_legislation.name: Wellbeing of Future Generations Bill 2025
dedicated_legislation.summary: Private member's bill introduced by Dr Sophie Scamps MP (independent). Directly inspired by Wales' Well-being of Future Generations Act. Proposes a Federal Wellbeing Framework, a duty for government and public bodies to consider long-term intergenerational wellbeing, a Future Generations Commissioner, and a National Conversation on future generations. Active civil society campaign led by Foundations for Tomorrow and the Intergenerational Fairness Coalition.

institutional_mechanisms.name: Australian Parliamentary Group for Future Generations
institutional_mechanisms.mandate: Cross-party parliamentary group established to advance law reform protecting future generations. Supports the Wellbeing of Future Generations Bill and advocates for a national Future Generations Commissioner. Not a statutory body — an informal parliamentary caucus.

institutional_mechanisms.name: Intergenerational Report (Treasury)
institutional_mechanisms.mandate: Required every five years under the Charter of Budget Honesty Act 1998. Projects the outlook for the economy and the federal budget over a 40-year horizon. The 2023 edition (Australia's future to 2063) incorporated a 'Measuring What Matters' wellbeing framework. Provides a long-term fiscal and economic lens, but does not carry enforceable intergenerational obligations.

institutional_mechanisms.name: Climate Change Authority
institutional_mechanisms.mandate: Independent body that advises the Australian Government on emissions targets and climate policy. Under the Climate Change Act 2022, it reports annually on progress toward Australia's climate targets. Its long-term reporting mandate serves intergenerational equity by providing accountability on multi-decade emissions pathways.

judicial_precedents.case: Sharma v Minister for the Environment [2021] FCA 560; [2022] FCAFC 35
judicial_precedents.court: Federal Court of Australia (trial); Full Federal Court (appeal)
judicial_precedents.relevance: Eight Australian children sued the federal Environment Minister, arguing she owed them a common law duty of care not to approve a coalmine extension that would contribute to climate harm. At trial (2021), Justice Bromberg found the Minister had a novel duty of care to protect children from climate harm — the first such finding globally, referencing the government's 'responsibility for the interests of future generations in the health of the environment.' On appeal (2022), the Full Federal Court unanimously overturned this, holding no such duty existed. Despite the reversal, the case catalysed global climate litigation and established that Australian courts would engage with intergenerational climate arguments.
judicial_precedents.outcome: Duty of care found at trial (2021); unanimously overturned on appeal (2022). No duty of care owed by the Minister.

international_commitments.instrument: UN Declaration on Future Generations (Pact for the Future, Annex II)
international_commitments.relevant_clause: Australia, as a UN member state, adopted the Declaration on Future Generations at the Summit of the Future on 22 September 2024. Commits states to safeguard the needs and interests of future generations.

international_commitments.instrument: Paris Agreement (UNFCCC)
international_commitments.relevant_clause: Australia ratified the Paris Agreement on 9 November 2016. Under the Albanese government, Australia submitted an updated NDC with a 43% emissions reduction target by 2030 and net-zero by 2050. The Paris Agreement's preamble acknowledges intergenerational equity.

policy_integration.mechanism: Intergenerational Report (Charter of Budget Honesty Act 1998)
policy_integration.description: Mandatory 40-year fiscal sustainability report required every five years under the Charter of Budget Honesty. The 2023 report incorporated a wellbeing framework alongside fiscal projections, marking an expansion into broader intergenerational policy considerations.

policy_integration.mechanism: Measuring What Matters Framework (2023)
policy_integration.description: National wellbeing framework launched by the Albanese government, tracking headline indicators across five themes: healthy, secure, sustainable, cohesive, and prosperous. Includes long-term sustainability indicators relevant to intergenerational equity. Not legislatively binding but represents integration of wellbeing into policy development.

policy_integration.mechanism: EPBC Act — Ecologically Sustainable Development Principles
policy_integration.description: The EPBC Act embeds intergenerational equity as a mandatory consideration in all environmental impact assessments and ministerial decisions on matters of national environmental significance. Decision-makers must consider whether proposed actions are consistent with the intergenerational equity principle.

countries.notes: Australia presents a dynamic and evolving picture. Its strongest asset is the EPBC Act's statutory intergenerational equity principle — one of the most explicit in the common law world — which applies to all national environmental decisions. The Sharma case was a near-miss: the first global judicial finding of a ministerial duty of care to future generations (overturned on appeal), but it accelerated climate litigation globally. The Wellbeing of Future Generations Bill 2025 is the most significant current development — a direct attempt to replicate Wales' WFGA with active civil society backing and a cross-party parliamentary group. The mandatory Intergenerational Report (40-year fiscal horizon) and the Measuring What Matters framework show growing policy integration. The main gap is a lack of constitutional recognition and the absence of a statutory future generations commissioner — both of which the 2025 Bill would address if passed.

constitutional_provisions.text: Mindful also of its responsibility toward future generations, the state shall protect the natural foundations of life and animals by legislation and, in accordance with law and justice, by executive and judicial action, all within the framework of the constitutional order.

dedicated_legislation.name: Jugend-Check (Kompetenzzentrum Jugend-Check / FÖV Speyer)
dedicated_legislation.scope: federal (administrative; every government draft law is pre-screened)
dedicated_legislation.status: active; Bundestag not bound to amend
dedicated_legislation.summary: Independent scientific unit funded by the federal youth ministry. Pre-screens every federal government draft; writes a published Jugend-Check when effects on ages 12–27 are identified (six life-domain screens). Third report of the 20th Bundestag: 490 bills screened, 91 published checks. This is a living-youth check, not an unborn-cohort IIA. Who can block: nobody.

dedicated_legislation.name: Federal Climate Change Act (Bundes-Klimaschutzgesetz)
dedicated_legislation.summary: Statutory emissions pathway. The Federal Constitutional Court's 2021 Neubauer decision required the legislature to specify post-2030 reductions so that later generations are not left with a radical duty. Climate law, not a pre-decision IIA annex.

institutional_mechanisms.name: Kompetenzzentrum Jugend-Check (KomJC)
institutional_mechanisms.mandate: Screens federal government drafts for intended and unintended effects on 12–27-year-olds, sends the check via BMFSFJ to the lead unit, and republishes if the cabinet text changes youth impacts. The Bundestag is not bound. KomJC itself warns that RefE-to-RegE changes cannot all be attributed to the check.

institutional_mechanisms.name: Projektstelle Jugend-Check Thüringen (ProJCT)
institutional_mechanisms.mandate: First German Land Jugend-Check, at FÖV Speyer, funded by the Thuringian social ministry. Publishes Land checks (ThürGDG, prisoner-pay, court organisation). Lead ministry decides whether to take results up. Not a Land statute.

institutional_mechanisms.name: No Future Generations Commissioner
institutional_mechanisms.mandate: Article 20a names future generations but creates no commissioner, ombudsperson, or statutory IIA. The Jugend-Check assesses present youth life situations, not unborn cohorts.

judicial_precedents.case: Neubauer et al. v. Germany (BVerfG, 24 March 2021, 1 BvR 2656/18)
judicial_precedents.relevance: The Court held that the Federal Climate Change Act's reduction path to 2030, without sufficient post-2030 specification, offloaded a radical mitigation burden onto later generations and thereby threatened their future freedom. Intergenerational constitutional doctrine, not a ruling that a missing Jugend-Check voids a bill.
judicial_precedents.outcome: Legislature required to set post-2030 reduction provisions by 31 December 2022.

international_commitments.instrument: UN Declaration on Future Generations (Pact for the Future, Annex II)
international_commitments.relevant_clause: Germany adopted the Declaration on Future Generations at the Summit of the Future (22 September 2024).

international_commitments.instrument: Paris Agreement (UNFCCC)
international_commitments.relevant_clause: Preamble acknowledges intergenerational equity. Neubauer used Basic Law Article 20a and fundamental-rights freedom over time rather than Paris as the operative duty.

international_commitments.instrument: EU Climate Law (Regulation 2021/1119)
international_commitments.relevant_clause: As an EU member state, Germany is bound by the European Climate Law net-zero 2050 pathway.

policy_integration.mechanism: Jugend-Check on minijobs / Mindestlohn package (2022) — skip
policy_integration.description: KomJC's 7 February 2022 Referentenentwurf check identified two youth-protective enforcement clauses (electronic hours record; payslip minimum-wage line). Both were deleted from the 23 February 2022 cabinet draft. Completed check, then skip.

policy_integration.mechanism: IKJHG RefE versus RegE (2024) — mixed; bill never enacted
policy_integration.description: Cabinet dropped a youth own-claim to out-of-home Hilfe zur Erziehung that KomJC flagged as strengthening adolescents' standing. Help-plan review interval moved in a youth-friendlier direction, without proven KomJC causation. IKJHG did not become law; a 2026 successor draft is a different bill.

policy_integration.mechanism: Thuringia Land Jugend-Check then enactment (court organisation, 2025)
policy_integration.description: Land check dated 29 July 2025 on the court-organisation bill; statute of 15 December 2025 (GVBl. 2025 Nr. 14) kept the Rechtspfleger Amtstracht clause already in the draft. Check-then-enact, not a rewrite. ThürGDG (8/3713) and prisoner-pay (8/3287) still pending in the Landtag as of 17 August 2026.

constitutional_recognition.detail: Article 20a names future generations; no dedicated IIA clause

dedicated_legislation.detail: Jugend-Check (admin) + Climate Change Act; no statutory IIA annex

policy_integration.detail: Checks are published; Bundestag not bound; documented skips

countries.notes: IIA deep dive: germany-intergenerational-equity. Jugend-Check is the densest published youth-IA series in the corpus (490/91) and the Bundestag is not bound. Bite pattern: skip (minijobs 2022) or check-then-enact (Thuringia robes). Not a future-unborn IIA.

constitutional_provisions.text: The Dutch Constitution does not name future generations as a justiciable class. Intergenerational claims in Dutch public law have travelled through ECHR Articles 2 and 8 (Urgenda) and through administrative policy tools (Beleidskompas generatietoets; Kinderrechtentoets), not through a Wales- or Italy-style constitutional entrenchment.

dedicated_legislation.name: Beleidskompas / Leidraad Toekomstgericht Beleid — generatietoets
dedicated_legislation.summary: The Rijksoverheid policy compass integrates a generatietoets at step 4 (consequences). After a generatiescan, a full toets is strongly advised when effects may redistribute burdens across generations, are irreversible, or lock later cohorts into costly-to-reverse choices. Outcomes are documented in beslisnota / memorie van toelichting. Nobody can void a bill for a missing toets. One of two national IIA-family instruments GYC classifies as enacted (with Italy VIG).

dedicated_legislation.name: Kinderrechtentoets (Kinderombudsman CRIA) — Senate youth-care instruction
dedicated_legislation.scope: national (youth-care bills; not a general statute)
dedicated_legislation.status: active instruction; methodology still being piloted
dedicated_legislation.summary: Eerste Kamer motion 36.546, I (7 October 2025) instructs government to apply the Kinderombudsman four-step child-rights impact assessment as standard on future jeugdzorg bills and record outcomes in the memorie van toelichting. The Kinderombudsman has no formal toetsingsrol. A later widening motion was rejected. This is a living-child CRIA cousin, not a future-unborn IIA.

dedicated_legislation.name: Climate Act (Klimaatwet) 2019
dedicated_legislation.summary: Statutory greenhouse-gas reduction pathway and climate-plan cycle. Not labelled an IIA, but the long-term carbon trajectory is the main statutory vehicle through which Dutch cabinets must account for later cohorts on climate.

institutional_mechanisms.name: Kinderombudsman
institutional_mechanisms.mandate: Promotes the Kinderrechtentoets toolkit, advises, and may brief Parliament. Has no power to stall a dossier or void a bill for a missing child-rights assessment.

institutional_mechanisms.name: Kenniscentrum voor beleid en regelgeving (KCBR) / BZK Beleidskompas
institutional_mechanisms.mandate: Hosts the Beleidskompas and points ministries to the Leidraad Toekomstgericht Beleid generatietoets. Method pages, not a commissioner.

institutional_mechanisms.name: No Future Generations Commissioner
institutional_mechanisms.mandate: The Netherlands has no Wales-style Future Generations Commissioner and no statutory Observatory of the Italian VIG type. Political pressure on the generatietoets travels through the Eerste Kamer (Miljoenennota motion 36.800 D).

judicial_precedents.case: Urgenda Foundation v. State of the Netherlands (Supreme Court, 20 December 2019)
judicial_precedents.relevance: Landmark climate duty-of-care ruling under ECHR Articles 2 and 8. The Court accepted that the State must protect residents from dangerous climate change, including by reducing emissions on a pathway that protects later cohorts. Not an IIA case: it does not require a pre-decision generatietoets, but it is the constitutional-adjacent backbone of Dutch intergenerational climate law.
judicial_precedents.outcome: State ordered to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by at least 25% by end-2020 versus 1990.

judicial_precedents.case: Milieudefensie v. Shell (Court of Appeal The Hague, 12 November 2024)
judicial_precedents.relevance: Corporate climate-duty appeal. Intergenerational framing is present in the climate-rights theory of the case; it is not a review of a missing generatietoets on a government bill.
judicial_precedents.outcome: Appeal judgment 12 November 2024; tracked in the foresight corpus.

international_commitments.instrument: UN Declaration on Future Generations (Pact for the Future, Annex II)
international_commitments.relevant_clause: The Netherlands adopted the Declaration on Future Generations at the Summit of the Future (22 September 2024).

international_commitments.instrument: Paris Agreement (UNFCCC)
international_commitments.relevant_clause: Preamble acknowledges intergenerational equity. Dutch climate litigation (Urgenda) used ECHR rather than Paris as the operative duty.

international_commitments.instrument: UN Convention on the Rights of the Child
international_commitments.relevant_clause: The Kinderrechtentoets is CRC-grounded (IVRK). It assesses living children, not unborn future generations as a separate legal person.

policy_integration.mechanism: Generatietoets on NPCE 2023–2030 (Sira, 18 December 2024)
policy_integration.description: First public completed generatietoets: contractor Sira Consulting scored the National Circular Economy Programme across nine themes × four living age bands × two horizons. Recommendations only; no primary evidence an NPCE measure was rewritten. Still the only Beleidskompas-era public worked example as of 17 August 2026.

policy_integration.mechanism: Senate Miljoenennota generatietoets motion (36.800 D) — skipped on MN 2026
policy_integration.description: Eerste Kamer adopted a motion instructing a generatietoets on the budget. Miljoenennota 2026 did not include one. Next public test is Prinsjesdag 15 September 2026 / Miljoenennota 2027.

policy_integration.mechanism: Wet reikwijdte Jeugdwet consultation Kinderrechtentoets (February 2026)
policy_integration.description: Only documented Dutch IIA-family amendment: consultation MvT §7.4 records two safeguards added after youth conversations (immediate extra jeugdhulp when necessary; usual-care test must allow help where parents cannot provide it). Not yet a statute. Minister Sterk's 20 May 2026 claim of a Kinderrechtentoets on Versterking jeugdbescherming is unverified against the public consultation MvT.

constitutional_recognition.detail: No Grondwet future-generations clause; ECHR/Urgenda is the live hook

dedicated_legislation.detail: 3 instruments: generatietoets (admin), Kinderrechtentoets instruction, Climate Act

institutional_mechanisms.detail: Kinderombudsman + KCBR method owner; no FG commissioner

judicial_enforcement.detail: Urgenda + Shell climate line; not IIA review

countries.notes: IIA deep dive: netherlands-intergenerational-equity. National generatietoets is enacted as administrative method, not a veto. Completing a toets is documented; changing a budget or bill is rare (one consultation-stage Kinderrechtentoets amendment). Next watch: Prinsjesdag 15 September 2026.

constitutional_provisions.article: Belgian Constitution — no national future-generations IIA clause
constitutional_provisions.text: Belgium has no federal statutory Intergenerational Impact Assessment and no constitutional commissioner for future generations. The live IIA-family instrument is Flemish: Jeugddecreet Article 7 JoKER (kind- en jongereneffectrapport), a child-and-youth effect report on Flemish Government draft decrees. Wallonia and the federal level have no equivalent enacted tool in the GYC corpus as of 17 August 2026.

dedicated_legislation.name: Flanders JoKER — Jeugddecreet Article 7 (kind- en jongereneffectrapport)
dedicated_legislation.status: active; age ceiling expanded to 30 on 13 March 2026
dedicated_legislation.summary: Every Flemish Government ontwerpdecreet that directly affects children and young people must carry a JoKER in the explanatory memorandum: effects with the measure, without it, and alternatives to avoid, limit or remedy serious harm. Not required on member bills, government decisions, ministerial orders or circulars. Who is assessed: persons through age 30 (tot en met 30) after the 13 March 2026 expansion. Unique in the IIA family: the Council of State can stall a dossier for a missing JoKER.

dedicated_legislation.name: Flemish decree expanding JoKER coverage from under-25 to age 30
dedicated_legislation.summary: Vlaams Parlement 754 (2025-2026) raised the JoKER population from under 25 to tot en met 30. Subsequent government bills must run the expanded screen. Completing JoKER after expansion does not automatically stall: bill 864 (27 May 2026, community-institution schools) filed a completed JoKER and the Council of State did not stall it.

institutional_mechanisms.name: Department of Culture, Youth and Media (CJM) — JoKER advice
institutional_mechanisms.mandate: The sponsoring Flemish minister and administration write the JoKER. CJM advises within 12 working days. This is not an independent KomJC-style checker.

institutional_mechanisms.name: Council of State (Raad van State / Conseil d'État) — Flemish legislation section
institutional_mechanisms.type: advisory / stall power on missing JoKER
institutional_mechanisms.mandate: Has required a missing JoKER before a Flemish youth-justice bill could proceed (opinion 69.100/1, 18 May 2021). That stall precedent is the only IIA-family instrument in the GYC corpus with documented dossier-blocking bite. Completing JoKER does not create a merits veto: the Council did not stall bill 864 after a completed report.

institutional_mechanisms.name: No federal Future Generations Commissioner or federal IIA
institutional_mechanisms.mandate: Federal Belgium has no enacted generational impact assessment, no Wales-style commissioner, and no Italy-style VIG. The IIA story in Belgium is Flanders JoKER plus Council of State procedure.

judicial_precedents.case: Council of State opinion 69.100/1 (18 May 2021) — missing JoKER on closed-supervision youth-justice bill
judicial_precedents.court: Raad van State / Conseil d'État (legislation section)
judicial_precedents.relevance: The Council required a missing JoKER before the 2021 closed-supervision youth-justice bill could proceed. The JoKER was written two days later. This is administrative-legislative procedure, not a constitutional-court merits review, and it is the stall precedent for the instrument.
judicial_precedents.outcome: Dossier stalled until JoKER filed; then proceeded.

international_commitments.instrument: UN Declaration on Future Generations (Pact for the Future, Annex II)
international_commitments.relevant_clause: Belgium adopted the Declaration on Future Generations at the Summit of the Future (22 September 2024).

international_commitments.instrument: UN Convention on the Rights of the Child
international_commitments.relevant_clause: JoKER is a child-and-youth effect report (through age 30 after March 2026), CRC-adjacent, not an unborn-cohort IIA.

international_commitments.instrument: Paris Agreement / EU Climate Law
international_commitments.relevant_clause: Belgium is bound as an EU member; those climate duties are separate from JoKER, which does not apply to federal climate bills.

policy_integration.mechanism: JoKER stall gate (CoS 69.100/1, 2021)
policy_integration.description: Only documented IIA-family stall: missing JoKER blocked a Flemish Government draft decree until the report was filed. Completing the form unblocks the dossier; it does not force the Council or Parliament to rewrite the policy.

policy_integration.mechanism: JoKER on bill 864 after age-30 expansion (27 May 2026) — no stall
policy_integration.description: Community-institution school bill filed a completed JoKER after the 13 March 2026 age-30 expansion. Council of State did not stall it. Completing JoKER is now routine; stalling is reserved for a missing report.

constitutional_recognition.detail: No national FG clause; Flemish JoKER is statutory at Community level

dedicated_legislation.detail: Jeugddecreet Art. 7 + 2026 age-30 expansion; federal IIA absent

institutional_mechanisms.detail: CJM advice + Council of State stall power

judicial_enforcement.detail: CoS procedure stall, not constitutional-court IIA review

countries.notes: IIA deep dive: belgium-intergenerational-equity. Belgium's IIA is Flanders JoKER, not a federal tool. Unique bite: Council of State can stall a missing report. Completing JoKER does not rewrite policy (bill 864, May 2026).

constitutional_provisions.text: The US federal Constitution does not explicitly mention future generations, intergenerational equity, or environmental rights. Some scholars argue the 14th Amendment's equal protection clause could extend to intergenerational equity, but this has not been accepted by federal courts.

dedicated_legislation.name: Future Generations Protection Act (H.R.6168, 117th Congress)
dedicated_legislation.summary: Introduced by Rep. Jan Schakowsky. Proposed to prohibit new fossil fuel extraction on federal lands, ban fracking, and establish a just transition framework. Did not advance out of committee.

dedicated_legislation.name: National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA)
dedicated_legislation.summary: Requires federal agencies to assess environmental impacts through Environmental Impact Statements. While not explicitly intergenerational, NEPA's long-term environmental analysis indirectly serves future generations.

institutional_mechanisms.name: Council on Environmental Quality (CEQ)
institutional_mechanisms.mandate: Oversees NEPA implementation. Not explicitly a future generations body, but its environmental review mandate serves intergenerational equity indirectly.

judicial_precedents.court: US District Court for Oregon; Ninth Circuit; US Supreme Court
judicial_precedents.relevance: 21 youth plaintiffs sued the federal government arguing climate change violates constitutional rights. Dismissed on standing grounds by Ninth Circuit (2020, 2024). Supreme Court denied certiorari March 2025, ending the case.

international_commitments.instrument: UN Declaration on Future Generations (Pact for the Future, Annex II)
international_commitments.relevant_clause: Adopted at Summit of the Future, September 2024. Commits states to safeguard needs and interests of future generations.

international_commitments.instrument: Paris Agreement (UNFCCC)
international_commitments.relevant_clause: Signed 2016, withdrew 2020, rejoined 2021. Status uncertain under current administration. Preamble acknowledges intergenerational equity.

policy_integration.mechanism: NEPA Environmental Impact Statements
policy_integration.description: Requires federal agencies to assess long-term environmental consequences of major actions. Does not explicitly require intergenerational impact analysis.

countries.notes: The US federal government has weak intergenerational equity frameworks: no constitutional provision, no dedicated legislation (bills failed), no commissioner, hostile federal courts (Juliana dismissed), and no intergenerational budgeting. The real action is at the state level — see individual state entries for Montana, Pennsylvania, Hawaii, New York, and others with green amendments and successful youth climate litigation.

constitutional_provisions.text: Federal budgeting is outcome-oriented. The child-and-youth dimension of the Wirkungsorientierte Folgenabschätzung is the live IIA-family instrument, not a constitutional future-generations clause.

dedicated_legislation.name: WFA-Kinder-und-Jugend-Verordnung (BGBl. II Nr. 495/2012)
dedicated_legislation.summary: Mandatory WFA Jugend-Check on all federal bills and major financially significant projects from 1 January 2013. Simplified screen, then a deeper assessment in material cases. Ministry self-assessment, not an independent checker. Who can block: must consider.

institutional_mechanisms.name: Sponsoring federal ministry (WFA author)
institutional_mechanisms.mandate: Writes the Kinder-und-Jugend WFA that travels with the government bill. Negative youth findings do not veto the measure.

international_commitments.instrument: UN Declaration on Future Generations
international_commitments.relevant_clause: Austria adopted the Declaration at the Summit of the Future.

policy_integration.mechanism: Budgetbegleitgesetz 2025 — completed WFA then skip
policy_integration.description: Government bill XXVIII/I/69 included completed child/youth WFA modules quantifying a two-year Familienbeihilfe freeze for two million children and a school-travel copay rise. Enacted as BGBl. I Nr. 25/2025. Bite: skip.

constitutional_recognition.detail: Budget outcome-orientation, not an FG clause

policy_integration.detail: Worked 2025 skip on the budget omnibus

countries.notes: IIA family lives on policy-tools.html#family=iia&country=AT. Mandatory cousin, documented skip.

constitutional_provisions.article: Charter for the Environment (2005) — no IIA clause
constitutional_provisions.text: France has no constitutional Intergenerational Impact Assessment. The live tool is an administrative youth-impact clause inside government impact studies.

dedicated_legislation.name: Clause d'impact jeunesse (circular 5857-SG, 2 May 2016)
dedicated_legislation.summary: Adds a youth-impact clause to études d'impact: equality among young people, intergenerational justice, non-discrimination. Ages 16–25 (25–30 flagged). Must consider, not a veto. Compensating measures expected if a text would penalise current or future young cohorts.

institutional_mechanisms.name: Secrétariat général du Gouvernement (SGG)
institutional_mechanisms.mandate: Hosts the mémento for enriched impact studies. Sponsoring ministries write the clause. Conseil d'orientation des politiques de jeunesse (COJ) reviews youth-relevant bills but is not a blocker.

international_commitments.instrument: UN Declaration on Future Generations
international_commitments.relevant_clause: France adopted the Declaration at the Summit of the Future.

policy_integration.mechanism: Loi 2025-268 agricultural orientation — youth-impact sections filled
policy_integration.description: The enacted agricultural law carried completed youth-impact clause sections. No proven article rewrite located. Bite: unknown.

countries.notes: IIA family lives on policy-tools.html#family=iia&country=FR. Cousin, bite unknown.

constitutional_provisions.text: For the benefit of present and future generations, the State and its political subdivisions shall conserve and protect Hawaii's natural beauty and all natural resources, including land, water, air, minerals and energy sources, and shall promote the development and utilization of these resources in a manner consistent with their conservation and in furtherance of the self-sufficiency of the State.

Each person has the right to a clean and healthful environment, as defined by laws relating to environmental quality, including control of pollution and conservation, protection and enhancement of natural resources. Any person may enforce this right against any party, public or private, through appropriate legal proceedings.

dedicated_legislation.name: Hawaii Environmental Policy Act (HEPA)
dedicated_legislation.summary: State-level NEPA equivalent requiring environmental impact statements for state and county actions. Hawaii's constitutional environmental provisions give HEPA stronger legal backing than NEPA has at the federal level.

institutional_mechanisms.name: Hawaii Office of Environmental Quality Control (OEQC)
institutional_mechanisms.mandate: Administers HEPA, reviews environmental impact statements, and serves as the state's environmental review body. Its mandate is implicitly intergenerational due to Hawaii's constitutional provisions.

judicial_precedents.case: In re Hawaii Electric Light Co. (2023)
judicial_precedents.relevance: The Hawaii Supreme Court denied a biomass power plant's application, citing the state's constitutional obligation to protect natural resources for present and future generations and the need to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. The ruling explicitly referenced Hawaii's constitutional commitment to future generations.
judicial_precedents.outcome: Power plant application denied on environmental and intergenerational grounds.

policy_integration.mechanism: Hawaii 2045 Zero Emissions Clean Economy Target (Act 15, 2018)
policy_integration.description: Hawaii committed to a zero emissions clean economy by 2045 — the most ambitious state-level climate target in the US. This long-term statutory commitment inherently serves intergenerational equity by locking in decarbonization pathways decades into the future.

countries.notes: Hawaii has one of the strongest constitutional environmental frameworks in the US, with two separate provisions explicitly protecting natural resources for 'present and future generations.' Combined with the nation's most ambitious statutory climate target (zero emissions by 2045), Hawaii integrates intergenerational equity into both its constitution and its policy framework.

constitutional_provisions.text: The state and each person shall maintain and improve a clean and healthful environment in Montana for present and future generations.
All persons are born free and have certain inalienable rights. They include the right to a clean and healthful environment...

dedicated_legislation.name: Montana Environmental Policy Act (MEPA)
dedicated_legislation.summary: State-level NEPA equivalent requiring environmental review of state actions. The 2023 legislature amended MEPA to bar consideration of climate impacts and greenhouse gas emissions in environmental reviews. The Montana Supreme Court in Held v. Montana (2024) struck down this limitation as unconstitutional, restoring MEPA's full environmental review scope.

institutional_mechanisms.name: Montana Department of Environmental Quality
institutional_mechanisms.mandate: State environmental regulatory agency responsible for implementing MEPA and enforcing environmental standards. Not explicitly a future generations body, but its mandate was strengthened by the Held v. Montana ruling requiring consideration of climate impacts.

judicial_precedents.court: Montana First Judicial District Court; affirmed by Montana Supreme Court (Dec 2024)
judicial_precedents.relevance: Landmark victory. 16 youth plaintiffs argued Montana's fossil fuel energy policies violated their constitutional right to a 'clean and healthful environment for present and future generations.' District Court ruled in August 2023 that the state's prohibition on considering climate impacts was unconstitutional. Montana Supreme Court affirmed in December 2024: youth have a 'fundamental constitutional right to a clean and healthful environment.' First US court to find a constitutional climate right for youth on the merits. Struck down two 2023 laws that limited MEPA.
judicial_precedents.outcome: Plaintiffs won. Montana Supreme Court affirmed. Two laws struck down.

policy_integration.mechanism: MEPA Environmental Review (restored full scope by Held v. Montana)
policy_integration.description: Following the Montana Supreme Court's ruling in Held, state agencies must now consider climate impacts and greenhouse gas emissions in environmental reviews under MEPA. This effectively integrates intergenerational climate considerations into state decision-making.

countries.notes: Montana is the strongest US state for intergenerational equity. Its 1972 constitution explicitly protects the environment for 'present and future generations' — language that proved decisive in Held v. Montana, the first US court victory establishing a constitutional climate right for youth. The Montana Supreme Court's 2024 affirmation is binding precedent within the state.

constitutional_provisions.text: Each person shall have a right to clean air and water, and a healthful environment.

dedicated_legislation.name: New York Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act (CLCPA)
dedicated_legislation.summary: One of the most ambitious state climate laws in the US. Mandates 40% reduction in greenhouse gas emissions by 2030 and 85% by 2050 (from 1990 levels), with net-zero by 2050. Requires at least 35% of climate investments benefit disadvantaged communities. While not explicitly framed as intergenerational, the long-term emissions targets inherently protect future generations.

institutional_mechanisms.name: New York Climate Action Council
institutional_mechanisms.mandate: Established by the CLCPA to develop a scoping plan for achieving the state's climate targets. Composed of state agency heads and community representatives. Its long-term planning mandate serves intergenerational equity indirectly.

policy_integration.mechanism: CLCPA Scoping Plan and Disadvantaged Communities mandate
policy_integration.description: The CLCPA requires a comprehensive scoping plan updated every five years, with mandatory consideration of disadvantaged communities. The 35% investment mandate for disadvantaged communities integrates equity considerations into climate policy implementation.

countries.notes: New York is the newest US state with a green amendment (2021). Its constitutional provision is less explicit about future generations than Montana or Pennsylvania, but combined with the CLCPA — one of the most ambitious state climate laws — it creates a strong framework. The green amendment has not yet been tested in major climate litigation.

constitutional_provisions.text: The people have a right to clean air, pure water, and to the preservation of the natural, scenic, historic and esthetic values of the environment. Pennsylvania's public natural resources are the common property of all the people, including generations yet to come. As trustee of these resources, the Commonwealth shall conserve and maintain them for the benefit of all the people.

institutional_mechanisms.name: Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection
institutional_mechanisms.mandate: State environmental regulatory agency. The Pennsylvania Supreme Court has interpreted Art. I, §27 as creating a public trust obligation, giving the DEP trustee responsibilities over natural resources for present and future generations.

judicial_precedents.relevance: Landmark ruling interpreting Pennsylvania's Environmental Rights Amendment. The court held that Art. I, §27 creates a public trust obligation and that the Commonwealth has fiduciary duties as trustee of public natural resources for 'generations yet to come.' Struck down parts of Act 13 (oil and gas law) as violating this trust obligation. Established that the amendment is self-executing and judicially enforceable.
judicial_precedents.outcome: Plaintiffs won. Act 13 partially struck down. Environmental Rights Amendment affirmed as enforceable public trust.

policy_integration.mechanism: Public Trust Doctrine via Art. I, §27
policy_integration.description: The Pennsylvania Supreme Court's Robinson Township ruling established that all state agencies and municipalities have trustee obligations under Art. I, §27 to conserve public natural resources for future generations. This creates a constitutional mandate for intergenerational consideration in all state resource decisions.

countries.notes: Pennsylvania was the first US state to adopt a green amendment (1971, one year before Montana). Its Environmental Rights Amendment is the strongest in the country in terms of explicit intergenerational language: 'including generations yet to come.' The Pennsylvania Supreme Court's Robinson Township ruling (2013) established that this creates enforceable public trust obligations — a powerful precedent for intergenerational equity litigation.
